The Story of Mrigasen the Fisherman

I bow with devotion to Lord Jinendra, whose eyes are omniscience, and I write the story of a fisherman who reaped the fruit of the vow of non-violence.

May the word of Lord Jinendra — which dispels all doubts, bestows every happiness upon those who worship with love — endure forever in this world. May the ocean of knowledge, the great monk who is like a bridge to carry noble souls across the fathomless ocean of existence, ever reside in my heart.

Having thus invoked the five supreme beings and sought auspiciousness, I write this sacred story of the vow of ahimsa to destroy the enemies known as karmas. The very name of ahimsa grants fearlessness to living beings, and its practice is undoubtedly the cause of happiness. Therefore, compassionate souls should abandon intentional violence in thought, word, and deed. Many commit violence in ancestral rituals, many sacrifice animals to please deities, and many kill creatures hoping to end epidemics and disease — but such violence brings not happiness but suffering. Those who imagine happiness through violence are simply ignorant. Sinful karma can never be the cause of happiness. True happiness lies in practising the vow of non-violence.

In the beautiful land of Surmya Avanti, in a small village called Shirish, there lived a fisherman named Mrigasen. One day, with a heavy net slung over his shoulder, he was heading to the Kshipra River to catch fish. On the way he beheld the monk Yashodhar. At that time many kings and nobles were worshipping at the monk's sacred feet. The sage was a great scholar of Syadvad, the fundamental doctrine of Jain philosophy, and was ever ready to uplift all living beings. His sole vow was the welfare of all creatures, and he had satisfied the entire world with the nectar of his religious discourse.

Mrigasen stood and listened to the sermon. The monk spoke of how every living being — from the smallest insect to the largest creature — desires life and fears death. He explained that violence binds heavy karmas to the soul and leads to endless suffering in future births. The fisherman's heart was transformed. He cast his net aside and fell at the monk's feet, vowing never to kill any creature again.

From that day forward, Mrigasen abandoned his profession of fishing. Though his family mocked him and neighbours laughed at his change of heart, he remained steadfast. He took up honest work and lived by the vow of ahimsa in thought, word, and deed. His mind grew peaceful, his conduct became pure, and through sincere practice of non-violence, he purified his soul and progressed on the path to liberation.

This story teaches that ahimsa is the supreme dharma. Even a fisherman, whose livelihood depended on killing, could renounce violence and walk the path of righteousness. No profession, no habit, no way of life is beyond reform when the heart is truly awakened to compassion.
